passage:
Monday. Bhupen, eleven, copied his maths homework from Rajat on the school bus. That evening, when his sister Alka spotted the same wrong answer in both books, he shrugged. "Everyone copies. And Sir gives way too much anyway."
Wednesday. Sir praised Bhupen's neat work in front of the class. Bhupen smiled, but at lunch he couldn't finish his paratha. "It's not cheating if it's just homework," he told Alka that night, though she hadn't said a thing.
Friday. He sat at the table with the new sums and a pencil. "I got question four wrong on my own," he told Alka. "That's okay, right?"

qa.q: Where did Bhupen copy his maths homework?
qa.a: On the school bus.

qa.q: Why did Bhupen say 'It's not cheating' when Alka hadn't said a thing?
qa.a: Bhupen wanted to keep seeing himself as a good kid, so reasons kept coming to quiet the uneasy feeling the copying left.

qa.q: What turning point came on Friday?
qa.a: Bhupen chose to do the sums himself and accept getting question four wrong, trading the excuses for honest work.

qa.q: How might Alka have seen Bhupen's excuses that week?
qa.a: Alka probably noticed the excuses came before she'd said anything, a sign that Bhupen felt uneasy about copying.

grounding: Over a week an eleven-year-old who copied homework piles up excuses that protect his good-kid image, then does the sums himself.

passage:
Sabina, you say everyone copies homework? Let your neighbour Karthik uncle tell you about Class 5, in 1978.
I copied my friend Selvam's English exercise every morning for a month. When my father found out, I had my reasons ready: everyone copies, Miss sets far too many exercises, and anyway English is useless for an engineer. I was very proud of those reasons. I thought they made me a good boy who was simply being clever.
Funny thing: I only thought of them after I'd copied. Never before.
Then came the half-yearly exam. No Selvam in the exam hall. I sat with the paper and could not write one sentence.
So. What were you really going to say about your homework?

qa.q: Whose English exercise did Karthik copy?
qa.a: His friend Selvam's.

qa.q: Why was young Karthik so proud of his reasons?
qa.a: The reasons let him keep seeing himself as a good boy who was just being clever, rather than someone who had copied.

qa.q: What might have helped young Karthik before the half-yearly exam?
qa.a: Doing even a few exercises on his own, and asking the teacher for help when there was too much, would have given him something to write in the exam.

qa.q: How might Sabina hear the question at the end?
qa.a: Sabina may feel gently caught, realising Karthik uncle has guessed that 'everyone copies' was an excuse, not the real story.

grounding: A neighbour recalls how as a boy his reasons for copying homework came only after the act and protected his image as a good boy.

passage:
The band for the wedding next door played until midnight, and Divyansh, ten, had spent the whole evening watching the dancers from the terrace instead of doing his science questions. In the morning, in the rattling school van, he copied Binita's answers on his knee.
When Binita asked, "Why didn't you do them yourself?", Divyansh had his answer ready. "Everyone copies science. Ma'am gives us twenty questions, that's crazy. And nobody could study with that band anyway."
"You could have done them before the band started," Binita said.
Divyansh looked out of the window. "I'm not a cheater. It's just homework," he said, a little too loudly.

qa.q: Where did Divyansh copy Binita's answers?
qa.a: In the rattling school van, on his knee.

qa.q: Why does Divyansh say 'I'm not a cheater' a little too loudly?
qa.a: Divyansh feels guilty and defensive about copying, so he piles up reasons to shield the picture of himself as a good kid.

qa.q: What could Divyansh do the next time an evening looks noisy?
qa.a: Start the science questions before the band begins, or tell Ma'am honestly if it's too much, instead of copying and explaining it away.

qa.q: How might Binita feel about being copied from and then argued with?
qa.a: Binita may feel used and a bit annoyed, since Divyansh took the answers and then blamed everything except himself.

grounding: On a noisy wedding night a ten-year-old skips his homework, copies in the school van, and then produces reasons to stay a good kid in his own eyes.

passage:
During lunch break at his school in Aliganj, Yusuf, ten, slid Abhinav's English worksheet under his own and copied the answers fast, pencil squeaking. His stomach gave a small twist.
That evening his cousin Rehana flipped through his bag and frowned. "These are exactly Abhinav's words."
"So?" Yusuf said, too quickly. "Everyone copies. Half the class copied from Abhinav. And Ma'am gives us four worksheets a day, it's crazy."
Rehana raised an eyebrow. Yusuf kept going. "I'm not a cheater. I'm top three in maths. I just didn't have time, that's all."
The more he explained, the better he felt. By dinner he had nearly convinced himself it was the only sensible thing to do. Still, when he packed his bag for school, he tucked the worksheet deep under his books.

qa.q: Where did Yusuf copy Abhinav's worksheet?
qa.a: During lunch break at his school in Aliganj, sliding it under his own.

qa.q: Why did Yusuf feel better the more he explained?
qa.a: Yusuf felt guilty after copying, and each reason he gave protected his picture of himself as a good student, so the guilt eased the more he explained.

qa.q: What moment could have been a turning point for Yusuf?
qa.a: When Rehana raised an eyebrow, Yusuf could have admitted copying and asked Ma'am for more time; instead he kept adding reasons.

qa.q: How might Rehana see Yusuf's list of reasons?
qa.a: Rehana probably notices that the reasons pile up only after being caught and come out too quickly, so they sound like a defence rather than the real story.

grounding: Shows a child who copied homework producing reasons afterwards, that everyone copies and there is too much work, to keep seeing himself as a good student.

passage:
Dear diary, Harsha here.

I copied Himani's maths homework on the bus today. All ten sums. It's not a big deal. Literally everyone copies. Neeraj copies every day and nobody says anything.

And Mrs Pinto gives SO much homework. Ten sums a night is too many for anyone. If she gave less, I wouldn't have had to.

Also I understood most of it anyway. I just didn't have time because of cricket. So it's basically like I did it.

Himani looked at me a bit funny when I gave her notebook back. Whatever.

I'm still a good student. I always get A's. One copy doesn't change that.

I'm going to sleep now. I don't feel bad. Much.

qa.a: All ten sums.

qa.q: Why does Harsha keep listing reasons after copying?
qa.a: Harsha feels a little guilty and wants to keep feeling like a good student, so the reasons arrive after the act to ease that uncomfortable feeling.

qa.q: What could Harsha try next time there's no time for homework?
qa.a: Harsha could tell Mrs Pinto honestly about the cricket clash and ask for help or a little extra time, instead of copying.

qa.a: Himani seems uneasy, looking at Harsha a bit funny, maybe unhappy to have her work copied.

passage: At the bus stop outside their village school near Moga, Anirban copied Amandeep's maths sums onto his own page, fast. The bus was late, and nobody saw. When Amandeep looked at him, Anirban said, "Everyone copies. Gurnoor copies every day." Amandeep said nothing. "And Masterji gives us too much. Twenty sums in one night? That's unfair." In class, Masterji ticked Anirban's page. "Good work." Anirban felt his ears go hot. He told himself: I'm a good boy, I help Bebe with the buffalo, I go to school every day. One copy doesn't matter. But on the way home, when Amandeep ran ahead to catch his cousin, Anirban kicked a stone for a long time. He didn't feel like a good boy. He felt like a boy with a secret.

qa.q: How many sums did Anirban say Masterji gave?
qa.a: Twenty sums in one night.

qa.q: Why did Anirban's ears go hot when Masterji said "Good work"?
qa.a: He felt guilty and ashamed, because the praise was for sums he had copied, and his excuses couldn't quite cover that.

qa.q: What would you advise Anirban to do now?
qa.a: He could tell Masterji the truth and ask for help with the sums he found hard, instead of adding more reasons.

qa.q: How might Amandeep see Anirban's excuses?
qa.a: Amandeep seems uncomfortable and unconvinced, staying silent and running ahead on the way home.

grounding: Shows a child who copied homework saying everyone copies and the teacher gives too much, reasons that protect his image of being good.

passage: In Buenos Aires, Mateo slid Ivan's science worksheet across the lunch table and copied the answers onto his own. "You're copying?" Ivan asked. "Everyone copies," Mateo said. "Lucas copied yesterday. And Señora Paz gives us way too much. Three worksheets a week? That's crazy." He finished and handed it back. "Anyway, I knew most of it. I just didn't have time." That afternoon Señora Paz returned the worksheets. Mateo got a gold star. He looked at it for a long time. His mother always said he was the honest one in the family. He shoved the worksheet deep into his bag. At home, when his mother asked about school, he said, "Fine," and went straight to his room.

qa.q: What did Mateo get on the worksheet?

qa.q: Why did Mateo shove the worksheet deep into his bag?
qa.a: He felt uncomfortable and guilty, because the gold star clashed with his picture of himself as the honest one.

qa.q: What could Mateo do to feel honest again?

qa.a: Ivan might feel doubtful and a little used, since his worksheet was copied and the excuses came only after.

Nitin copied the last four maths sums from Yamini's notebook in the school library, ten minutes before the bell, hunched behind a shelf of atlases. Only afterwards, walking back to class, did the reasons come.

"Everybody copies," he told Yamini. "Half the class copied from Ronak yesterday."

Yamini frowned. "I didn't."

"Well, Kulkarni ma'am gives way too much. Twenty sums! That's not fair on anyone." He was talking fast now. "And I did the first sixteen myself. So it's basically mine."

"Then why did you hide behind the atlases?" Yamini asked.

Nitin opened his mouth, closed it, and looked at his shoes. "I'm not a cheater," he said quietly. "I always do my homework."

passage:
Suraj, come, sit. You think your Dada Tanvir was a perfect boy? Listen. When I was about your age, in Class Five in Aligarh, our teacher, Masterji Rahmat, gave us twenty sums every night. One evening I played gilli-danda till dark, and in the morning I copied my friend Irshad's page in the courtyard. Masterji didn't notice.

But at home I told my mother, "Everyone copies, Ammi. And Masterji gives too much. What's the point of twenty sums?" I said it three times. She only asked, "If it's fine, why are you telling me three times?"

I had no answer. The next night I did the sums myself, badly, with ink on my fingers. Remember that question, Suraj. It helped me more than any sum.

qa.q: What did young Tanvir play until dark?
qa.a: Tanvir played gilli-danda till dark.

qa.q: Why did young Tanvir keep repeating the reasons to Ammi?
qa.a: Young Tanvir felt guilty inside and wanted to stay a good boy in Ammi's eyes, so saying the reasons again helped quiet that uneasy feeling.

qa.q: What was the turning point in the story, and why did it matter?
qa.a: Ammi's question about saying it three times made Tanvir see the reasons were covering something, and the next night he did the sums himself.

qa.q: How might Ammi have seen her son's excuses that day?
qa.a: Ammi probably saw through them gently; instead of scolding, she asked one question that let Tanvir notice the truth himself.

grounding: A grandfather recalls copying a friend's sums as a boy and piling up excuses afterwards until his mother's question made him stop.

passage: On a foggy winter morning, the school bus crawled along, and Sarita suddenly remembered the maths homework she hadn't done. With fifteen minutes left, she copied every answer from Seema's notebook, bumping along on the seat. In class the teacher noticed the identical mistakes. "Sarita, did you copy?" Sarita's face went hot. "Everyone copies, Miss. And you give too much homework anyway. And the bus was late." The reasons tumbled out one after another, faster than she could think them. At home she said it again to her grandmother: everyone does it. Her grandmother asked, "Did you think 'everyone does it' before you copied, or after?" Sarita was quiet. It was after. Before, she had only thought, quick, before we get there.

qa.a: Seema's.

qa.q: Why did the reasons tumble out so fast?
qa.a: Sarita felt ashamed and hot-faced, and the excuses protected her picture of herself as a good student.

qa.q: What did her grandmother's question show Sarita?
qa.a: That the reasons came after the copying, not before; seeing that could help her admit it and plan to do homework on time.

qa.q: How might Seema be affected?
qa.a: Seema could get into trouble too because of the identical mistakes, and might feel used.

During the Christmas holidays we got a whole booklet of maths sums. On the last evening I still hadn't done page six, so I copied it from Keerthana's photo in our class group. When Amma asked, I said, "Everyone copies, Amma. Even the toppers." And Sir sets way too many anyway, right? Who does forty sums in a holiday?
I told myself that all night. I'm a good student, mostly. I help people. So one page didn't count.
But on Monday, when Sir praised page six and said, "Well done, Jagdish," my ears went hot, and I didn't look at Keerthana.
